title: DNS, DHCP and name resolution
summary: Discover how DHCP automatically hands out IP addresses and how DNS turns human-friendly names into IP addresses, plus the tools to test both.
objectives: Explain what DHCP does and the DORA lease process
Describe how DNS resolves a name to an IP address
Identify common DNS record types like A, AAAA, CNAME and MX
Use nslookup to query DNS from the command line
Recognise symptoms of DHCP and DNS failures on the helpdesk
Flush and renew network settings on Windows

quiz.q: What does a DHCP server provide to a client?
options: An IP address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS servers
quiz.why: DHCP automatically leases a client its IP configuration: address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server addresses.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the DHCP lease process?
quiz.why: The DORA process runs Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge — the client discovers, the server offers, the client requests, the server acknowledges.
DNS resolves human-friendly domain names like example.com into the numeric IP addresses computers use to connect.

quiz.q: Which DNS record maps a name to an IPv4 address?
quiz.why: An A record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address; AAAA does the same for IPv6, and MX points to mail servers.

quiz.q: Name the command that queries DNS to resolve a name on Windows.
quiz.why: nslookup (or dig on Linux/macOS) sends a DNS query and shows the IP address a name resolves to, which is essential for diagnosing name resolution faults.

quiz.q: In one sentence, how would you tell a DNS problem from a connectivity problem?
quiz.answer: If you can ping a public IP like 8.8.8.8 but cannot reach a website by name, connectivity is fine and DNS is the problem.
quiz.why: Pinging by IP bypasses DNS, so success by IP but failure by name isolates the fault to name resolution rather than the network link.

body_markdown:
## Two services that make networks usable

Imagine setting a unique IP address by hand on every device, and memorising the IP of every website. Painful. Two services rescue us: **DHCP**, which hands out IP addresses automatically, and **DNS**, which turns names like `example.com` into IP addresses. They run quietly in the background, but when either fails, the helpdesk phone rings.

## DHCP: automatic addressing

**DHCP** (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) leases each device its full IP configuration: an **IP address**, a **subnet mask**, a **default gateway**, and **DNS server** addresses. The handshake is remembered with the word **DORA**:

- **Discover** — the client shouts "is there a DHCP server?"
- **Offer** — a server replies with an available address.
- **Request** — the client says "I'll take it."
- **Acknowledge** — the server confirms and records the **lease**.

If no server answers, the client falls back to an **APIPA** address (`169.254.x.x`) and has no real connectivity.

## DNS: the internet's phone book

**DNS** (Domain Name System) translates names into IP addresses. When you type a website, your PC asks a **resolver**, which works down from the **root** servers to the **top-level domain** (like `.com`), to the domain's **authoritative** server, and gets back an IP. The result is cached so the next lookup is instant.

Common **record types** you should recognise:

```text
A      name -> IPv4 address
AAAA   name -> IPv6 address
CNAME  name -> another name (an alias)
MX     domain -> mail server
TXT    free text, used for verification (SPF, etc.)
```

## Testing name resolution

The key tool is **nslookup** (or `dig` on macOS/Linux):

```bash
nslookup example.com

Server:   192.168.1.1
Address:  192.168.1.1#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:     example.com
Address:  93.184.216.34
```

That tells you which DNS server answered and the IP it returned. If `nslookup` fails but `ping 8.8.8.8` works, you have a **DNS problem**, not a connectivity problem.

## Fixing common faults

Most DHCP and DNS issues clear with three Windows commands: release and renew the DHCP lease, and flush the DNS cache.

```bash
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew
ipconfig /flushdns
```

A stale or poisoned DNS cache can make one site unreachable while others work — `flushdns` is the first thing to try. If a PC shows a `169.254.x.x` address after `/renew`, suspect the DHCP server or the cable.

## Your task

Run `nslookup example.com` and note the DNS server that answered and the IP returned. Then run `nslookup` on your own company or school website. Finally, run `ipconfig /flushdns` and confirm it reports the cache was cleared. Write down, in your own words, how you would tell a DNS fault apart from a connectivity fault.

Today we meet the two invisible services that make networks actually usable for humans: D H C P, which hands out addresses automatically, and D N S, which turns website names into addresses. When these break, the phone rings, so understanding them is core helpdesk knowledge.

slides.narration: Let's start with D H C P, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. It leases each device its full configuration: an I P address, a subnet mask, a default gateway, and the addresses of D N S servers. Everything a device needs to talk on the network. If no D H C P server answers, the device falls back to that one sixty-nine dot two fifty-four APIPA address we met last time, and it has no real connectivity.

slides.title: The DORA process
bullets: Discover: client asks if any DHCP server is there.
Offer: a server offers an available address.
Request: client says it will take that address.
Acknowledge: server confirms and records the lease.
slides.narration: The D H C P handshake is easy to remember with the word DORA. D, Discover: the client shouts, is there a D H C P server out there? O, Offer: a server replies with an available address. R, Request: the client says, I'll take it please. And A, Acknowledge: the server confirms and writes down the lease. Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. DORA.

slides.title: DNS: the internet's phone book
bullets: DNS translates names into IP addresses.
Your PC asks a resolver, which works down the tree.
Root, then top-level domain, then authoritative server.
Results are cached so the next lookup is instant.
slides.narration: Now D N S, the Domain Name System, the internet's phone book. When you type a website name, your P C asks a resolver. That resolver works down a tree: first the root servers, then the top-level domain like dot com, then the domain's own authoritative server, and back comes the I P address. The answer gets cached, so the next time you visit, the lookup is instant.

slides.title: DNS record types
bullets: A record: name to an IPv4 address.
AAAA record: name to an IPv6 address.
CNAME: an alias, one name pointing to another.
MX: points a domain to its mail server.
slides.code:
A      name -> IPv4
AAAA   name -> IPv6
CNAME  name -> another name
MX     domain -> mail server
slides.narration: D N S stores different record types, and you should know the main ones. An A record maps a name to an I P version four address. A quad-A record does the same for I P version six. A C name record is an alias, one name pointing at another name. And an M X record points a domain to its mail server. When email won't deliver, the M X record is often where you look first.

slides.title: Testing with nslookup
bullets: nslookup queries DNS from the command line.
It shows which server answered and the IP returned.
Use dig on macOS and Linux for the same job.
Works by IP but not by name = a DNS problem.
slides.narration: Your key tool here is n s lookup, or dig on Mac and Linux. Type n s lookup and a website name. It tells you which D N S server answered and the I P address it returned. Here's the golden rule for the helpdesk: if you can ping eight dot eight dot eight dot eight but n s lookup fails, you have a D N S problem, not a connectivity problem. Pinging by I P bypasses D N S entirely.

slides.title: Fixing common faults
bullets: Release and renew the DHCP lease.
Flush the DNS cache to clear stale entries.
flushdns is the first thing to try for one bad site.
APIPA after renew points to DHCP or the cable.
slides.narration: Most D H C P and D N S problems clear with three commands. I p config slash release and slash renew get a fresh address from the D H C P server. And i p config slash flush d n s clears the local D N S cache. A stale cached entry can make one site unreachable while everything else works, so flush d n s is your first move. And if a P C still shows a one sixty-nine address after renewing, suspect the D H C P server or a bad cable.
